rc.title: Impressionism and the Paint Tube
paras: Art historians usually explain the emergence of Impressionism in nineteenth-century France by pointing to the artists' rebellion against the rigid standards of the official Salon, or to their fascination with new scientific theories of light and color. Less often mentioned, but arguably just as important, is a humble invention: the collapsible metal paint tube.

Before the 1840s, painters who wished to work outdoors faced considerable practical obstacles. Paint was typically prepared in the studio by grinding pigments by hand and mixing them with oil, and it was stored in small bags made of animal bladder that were difficult to seal and tended to burst. Consequently, most landscapes were painted indoors, on the basis of sketches made on location. The metal tube, patented in 1841 by an American portrait painter living in London, changed this situation. Paint could now be carried easily, kept fresh for long periods and squeezed out in precise quantities.

The tube also encouraged the introduction of new, brilliant pigments, which manufacturers could now sell ready-made. For the young artists who would later be called Impressionists, these developments made it possible to paint an entire canvas in the open air, capturing the fleeting effects of sunlight on water or foliage before they changed. Pierre-Auguste Renoir is said to have remarked that without paint in tubes there would have been no Impressionism.

Of course, technology alone does not create an artistic movement. Many painters of the period had access to tubes, yet only a few chose to use them in such radical ways. The tube did not dictate a new style; rather, it removed a barrier, allowing artists who already wished to break with tradition to do so more freely.

rc.title: Endangered Languages
paras: Of the roughly seven thousand languages spoken in the world today, linguists estimate that as many as half may no longer be spoken by the end of this century. Most of these endangered languages have only a few thousand speakers, and many have far fewer. When the last fluent speaker of such a language dies, a unique system of sounds, words and grammar disappears as well.

Languages rarely die because their speakers are wiped out. Far more commonly, a community gradually shifts to a more dominant language, one used in schools, government and the media and associated with economic opportunity. Parents may decide that their children will be better off speaking the majority language, and within two or three generations the original language survives only among the elderly.

Linguists regard this loss as serious for several reasons. Each language encodes a particular way of organizing experience; some languages, for instance, describe the location of objects using compass directions rather than words like left and right. Languages also preserve knowledge about local plants, animals and landscapes that may not be recorded anywhere else. For the communities themselves, moreover, the language is often closely bound up with identity and tradition.

Decline, however, is not always irreversible. Hebrew, which for centuries was used mainly in prayer and study, was revived as an everyday spoken language in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries and now has millions of native speakers. Welsh and Maori have also gained new speakers through school programs and broadcasting. Such cases remain exceptional, but they demonstrate that determined communities can reverse the decline of a language.

rc.title: Reading History in Tree Rings
paras: Every year, a tree in a temperate climate adds a new layer of wood beneath its bark. In spring the tree produces wide, pale cells; later, growth slows and the cells become smaller and darker. The result is a series of rings, one for each year of the tree's life. In the early twentieth century, an American astronomer named Andrew Ellicott Douglass, who was studying the effect of sunspots on climate, realized that these rings could serve as a remarkably precise calendar.

The key to the method is that rings are not all the same width. In a wet year a tree grows generously and lays down a thick ring; in a year of drought the ring may be barely visible. Because all the trees in a region experience the same weather, they share the same pattern of thick and thin rings. By matching the patterns of living trees with those of older timber, researchers can extend the record far beyond the life of any single tree. In parts of Europe, such sequences now reach back over ten thousand years.

For archaeologists, this has proved invaluable. A wooden beam from an ancient house or a plank from a shipwreck can be compared with the master sequence, and if the pattern fits, the year in which the tree was cut down can often be identified exactly. In the American Southwest, Douglass himself used the technique to date the cliff dwellings of the Ancestral Pueblo people, settling a question that had puzzled scholars for decades.

The method does have limits. It works best in regions with marked seasons, since trees in the tropics often grow all year round and form no clear rings. Moreover, a beam reveals only when its tree died, not when the wood was used; builders sometimes reused old timber, which can make a structure appear older than it really is. Even so, tree-ring dating remains one of the most accurate tools available to those who study the past.

rc.title: Shadows Across Distant Suns
paras: For most of human history, the existence of planets orbiting other stars was a matter of philosophical speculation rather than observation. The difficulty is easy to state: a planet is billions of times fainter than the star it circles and, seen from Earth, lies so close to it that its feeble light is overwhelmed by the star's glare. Directly photographing such a world has therefore been, until very recently, all but impossible, and astronomers have had to devise indirect means of inferring its presence.

The most productive of these is the transit method. If a planet's orbit happens to be aligned so that, from our vantage point, it passes in front of its star, it blocks a minute fraction of the star's light. A planet the size of Jupiter crossing a Sun-like star dims it by roughly one percent; an Earth-sized planet, by less than one hundredth of a percent. By monitoring the brightness of many thousands of stars simultaneously, space telescopes such as Kepler, launched in 2009, have detected these periodic dips and thereby identified thousands of planets.

The technique yields more than a mere census. The depth of each dip reveals the planet's size relative to its star, and the interval between dips gives the length of its year. Furthermore, when starlight passes through the atmosphere of a transiting planet, certain wavelengths are absorbed by the gases present, so that careful analysis of the filtered light can disclose the atmosphere's chemical composition, a feat that would have seemed fanciful a generation ago.

Yet the method is inherently biased. Only planets whose orbits are nearly edge-on to us produce transits at all, and large planets in tight orbits, which transit frequently and conspicuously, are far easier to detect than small ones that circle their stars slowly. Consequently, the catalogue of known planets cannot be taken as a faithful portrait of the galaxy's planetary population; astronomers must correct statistically for the many worlds the method is bound to miss.

rc.title: The Doctor Who Washed His Hands
paras: In the 1840s, the Vienna General Hospital ran two maternity clinics side by side. Women who gave birth in the first clinic, which was staffed by doctors and medical students, died of a disease called childbed fever at a far higher rate than those in the second, which was staffed by midwives. The difference was so well known that some women begged to be admitted to the second clinic, and a few even preferred to give birth in the street.

Ignaz Semmelweis, a young Hungarian doctor working in the first clinic, set out to discover why. He ruled out one explanation after another, including overcrowding and the climate, which were the same in both clinics. The breakthrough came in 1847, when a colleague died after being cut accidentally during an autopsy, showing symptoms very similar to those of the dying mothers. Semmelweis concluded that doctors, who often came to the delivery room directly from dissecting dead bodies, were carrying harmful particles on their hands.

He ordered all staff to wash their hands in a solution of chlorinated lime before examining patients. The results were dramatic: within months, the death rate in the first clinic fell to roughly the level of the second. Yet many of his colleagues rejected his conclusions. Some were offended by the suggestion that doctors themselves were causing harm, and Semmelweis, who could not explain the mechanism behind his findings, did little to win them over; he published his results late and often attacked his critics in angry letters.

Semmelweis died in 1865, largely ignored. Only in the following decades, when Louis Pasteur and others showed that many diseases are caused by microorganisms, did his ideas gain general acceptance. Today he is honored as a pioneer of hospital hygiene, and his story is often told as a warning about the danger of dismissing evidence simply because it is uncomfortable.

rc.title: The Weight of an Arbitrary Number
paras: Economic theory has traditionally assumed that people arrive at judgments of value by weighing the relevant information available to them. A substantial body of research in behavioral economics, however, suggests that our estimates are often tethered to whatever number we happened to encounter first, even when that number is patently irrelevant. This tendency, which the psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman termed "anchoring," ranks among the most robust findings in the study of human judgment.

In one of their best-known demonstrations, participants watched a wheel of fortune, rigged to stop at either 10 or 65, and were then asked to estimate the percentage of African nations in the United Nations. Those who had seen the higher number gave substantially higher estimates, typically 45 percent as opposed to 25 percent, although the wheel could not conceivably have conveyed any information about the question. Subsequent studies have replicated the effect with judges determining sentences, estate agents appraising houses, and shoppers deciding how much they would pay for ordinary goods.

Researchers continue to debate why anchors exert such influence. One account holds that people start from the anchor and adjust away from it, but stop prematurely, once they reach a value that seems plausible. Another proposes that an anchor selectively brings to mind information consistent with it: considering whether a house might be worth a high figure prompts one to recall its attractive features rather than its defects. The two explanations are not mutually exclusive, and each may predominate under different circumstances.

The practical implications are considerable. Negotiators who make the first offer frequently secure better outcomes, since the opening figure frames the subsequent discussion, and retailers display an inflated "original price" beside a sale price for much the same reason. Notably, warning people about the bias appears to reduce it only slightly, which suggests that anchoring operates largely below the level of conscious deliberation.

rc.title: The Stone Skeleton of the Gothic Cathedral
paras: Visitors who enter a Gothic cathedral for the first time are often struck by two things: the remarkable height of the interior and the flood of colored light pouring through enormous windows. Both features were made possible by a structural innovation that is easy to overlook, because much of it stands outside the building: the flying buttress.

To understand its importance, one must consider the problem faced by medieval builders. A heavy stone vault does not merely press down on the walls that support it; it also pushes them outward. In the earlier Romanesque style, this outward force was resisted by making the walls extremely thick and keeping the windows small, which is why Romanesque churches tend to be massive and dim inside. The higher a vault was raised, the greater the danger that the walls would be forced apart and the roof would collapse.

The flying buttress offered an elegant solution. It is a half-arch of stone that springs from the upper part of the wall and carries the outward thrust across open air to a heavy pier standing some distance from the building. Because the wall no longer had to bear this force alone, it could be made thinner and opened up with large windows of stained glass. Builders in northern France began using the device in the twelfth century, and it soon spread across Europe.

Not every experiment succeeded. At Beauvais, where builders attempted the tallest choir ever constructed, part of the vault collapsed in 1284, only twelve years after it was completed. Such failures remind us that the cathedral builders worked without mathematical theories of structure, relying instead on experience, tradition and a willingness to take risks. That so many of their buildings still stand is a tribute to their skill.

rc.title: Why Some Newcomers Run Wild
paras: Of the many species that humans transport, deliberately or accidentally, beyond their native ranges, the great majority either fail to establish themselves or persist as inconspicuous members of their new communities. A small proportion, however, proliferate explosively, displacing native species and transforming entire ecosystems. Explaining why particular introductions become invasive, while most do not, has become one of the central problems of modern ecology.

One influential explanation is the "enemy release hypothesis." In its native habitat, every species is kept in check by predators, parasites and diseases that have evolved alongside it. When a plant or animal is carried to a distant continent, it typically leaves most of these enemies behind, while the native organisms it encounters have not yet adapted to exploit it. Freed from the pressures that once restrained it, the newcomer can devote more of its resources to growth and reproduction.

There is considerable evidence for this view. Surveys have found that introduced plants are, on average, attacked by fewer species of fungi and viruses in their new ranges than in their native ones, and that some, such as purple loosestrife in North America, have been brought under control only after insects that feed on them in Europe were deliberately released. Nonetheless, the hypothesis is far from a complete account. Many species that escape their enemies never become invasive, and some invaders thrive despite being heavily attacked.

Ecologists increasingly argue that invasion results from a combination of factors rather than a single cause. The characteristics of the invader, such as rapid reproduction, may interact with those of the receiving ecosystem, which may already have been disturbed by agriculture or construction. Furthermore, success may depend on sheer numbers: species introduced repeatedly and in large quantities are markedly more likely to establish themselves than those released once in small groups.

rc.title: Learning While We Sleep
paras: For centuries, sleep was regarded as a period in which the brain simply rested, switching off like a machine at the end of the working day. Research over the past few decades has overturned this view. We now know that the sleeping brain is extremely active, and that one of its most important tasks is to strengthen the memories formed during the day.

Some of the clearest evidence comes from experiments with rats. When a rat learns its way through a maze, particular cells in a region of the brain called the hippocampus fire in a specific order as the animal passes each point along the route. Researchers who recorded the activity of these cells discovered that the same sequence was repeated during the rat's sleep that night, often at a much faster speed, as if the brain were rehearsing the route.

Studies with human volunteers point in the same direction. In a typical experiment, people learn a list of word pairs or practice a sequence of finger movements and are tested again twelve hours later. Those whose twelve hours included a night's sleep usually perform better than those who spent the same period awake. Interestingly, different stages of sleep appear to support different kinds of memory: deep sleep seems especially important for facts, while the stage in which most dreaming occurs may help more with skills and emotional memories.

These findings have practical consequences. Students who stay up all night before an examination may be undermining the very learning they hope to achieve, since without sleep newly acquired information is less likely to be retained. Scientists are also investigating whether poor sleep in old age contributes to the memory problems that many elderly people experience.

rc.title: The Test as a Teacher
paras: In most educational systems, tests are regarded primarily as instruments of measurement: they are administered at the end of a unit to determine how much students have learned, much as a thermometer registers a temperature without altering it. A growing body of research in cognitive psychology challenges this assumption. The act of retrieving information from memory, it turns out, does not merely reveal learning; it actively strengthens it, a phenomenon known as the testing effect.

In a frequently cited study, students read a short scientific passage and were then assigned either to reread it several times or to read it once and attempt to recall as much as they could on blank paper. When tested five minutes later, the rereaders performed slightly better. A week later, however, the pattern was reversed: those who had practiced recall remembered considerably more, even though they had spent less time with the material. Strikingly, the rereaders were more confident that they would remember the passage well.

This discrepancy between confidence and performance helps explain why students persist in favoring ineffective strategies. Rereading produces a feeling of fluency, as the text seems increasingly familiar, and this feeling is easily mistaken for mastery. Retrieval, by contrast, is effortful and often frustrating, since it exposes gaps in one's knowledge. Yet it is precisely this difficulty that appears to make it beneficial, an instance of what researchers call "desirable difficulties."

Advocates of retrieval practice do not contend that more frequent high-stakes examinations are the answer; anxiety about grades may well offset any gains. Rather, they recommend brief, low-stakes quizzes, flashcards and practice questions integrated into ordinary study. Some caution is warranted, nonetheless: most experiments have used relatively simple material, and whether the benefits extend fully to complex reasoning tasks remains a matter of ongoing investigation.

rc.title: The Search for a Standard Pitch
paras: When an orchestra tunes before a concert, the oboe plays a single note, and the other musicians adjust their instruments to match it. In most of the world today that note, the A above middle C, vibrates 440 times per second. This agreement may seem natural, but it is surprisingly recent. For most of the history of Western music, there was no common standard at all.

In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, the pitch of A varied enormously from city to city and even from church to church. An organ in one German town might be tuned almost a whole tone higher than an organ a few miles away. Musicians who travelled had to adapt constantly, and singers sometimes found that a piece which was comfortable in one place was nearly impossible to perform in another.

During the nineteenth century the problem took a new form. Orchestras gradually raised their pitch, partly because a higher tuning made instruments sound brighter and more brilliant in large concert halls. Singers complained that the rising pitch was straining their voices. In 1859, the French government responded by passing a law that fixed A at 435 vibrations per second, and several other countries later adopted the same figure.

The modern standard of 440 was recommended by an international conference held in London in 1939, and it was confirmed by the International Organization for Standardization in 1955. Even so, the matter is not entirely settled. Some modern orchestras tune slightly higher, to 442 or 443, while performers of early music often prefer lower pitches, believing that these come closer to the sound the composers themselves would have heard.

rc.title: Gifts That Bind
paras: In the early twentieth century, the anthropologist Bronisław Malinowski spent several years among the Trobriand Islanders off the eastern coast of New Guinea. Among the institutions he documented, none intrigued him more than the kula, a system of ceremonial exchange in which men undertook long and hazardous canoe voyages to neighboring islands in order to present and receive objects of shell. Necklaces of red shell circulated around the ring of islands in one direction, while armbands of white shell travelled in the other.

What puzzled Western observers was that these valuables had no practical use and were seldom kept for long. A man who received a celebrated necklace would hold it for a time, gaining prestige from its possession, and then pass it on to a partner, often on another island. The objects were thus valued not as property to be accumulated but as tokens whose worth lay in their histories, in the names of the prominent men who had once held them.

Malinowski argued that the kula could not be understood through the categories of market economics. Partners did not haggle; indeed, haggling over kula valuables was considered shameful, and a gift was answered by a counter-gift only after an interval, sometimes of many months. The exchange created enduring obligations between partners, and these relationships in turn facilitated the ordinary trade in food and goods that accompanied the expeditions.

Later scholars, most notably Marcel Mauss, drew on such accounts to propose that gift exchange is a fundamental mechanism of social life, binding people through the obligation to give, to receive and to reciprocate. Critics have since cautioned against romanticizing such systems, observing that the kula also served as an arena of fierce competition for status. Still, the broader insight endures: exchange can be as much about creating relationships as about acquiring things.

rc.title: The Table That Predicted the Future
paras: By the middle of the nineteenth century, chemists had identified more than sixty elements, from familiar metals such as iron and copper to more recently discovered substances like lithium. They knew a great deal about how each element behaved, but they lacked a system that could show how the elements were related to one another. Several scientists tried to arrange them in a meaningful order, yet none of their schemes won general acceptance.

In 1869 the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev published a table that arranged the known elements in order of increasing atomic weight, placing elements with similar properties in the same column. This in itself was not entirely new. What made Mendeleev's table different was his willingness to leave gaps in it. When the next element in order of weight did not fit the pattern, he did not force it into the wrong place; instead, he assumed that an undiscovered element belonged there.

Mendeleev went further, predicting the properties of several of these missing elements in remarkable detail. For one, which he called "eka-aluminium," he estimated its weight, its density and the kinds of compounds it would form. In 1875 a French chemist discovered a new metal, gallium, whose properties matched the prediction closely. Two other predicted elements, later named scandium and germanium, were found within the next eleven years.

These successes persuaded the scientific world that the periodic table reflected something real about the structure of matter, even though no one could yet explain why the pattern existed. That explanation came only in the twentieth century, with the discovery of the atom's internal structure. Today the table hangs in nearly every chemistry classroom, a lasting reminder that a good theory not only organizes what is known but also points the way to what is not.

rc.title: Why New Roads Fill Up
paras: For much of the twentieth century, transportation planners treated traffic congestion as a straightforward problem of supply and demand: if roads were crowded, the remedy was to build more of them. Highways were widened, new lanes were added, and bypasses were constructed around clogged city centers, all on the assumption that the volume of traffic was essentially fixed and that additional capacity would allow it to flow freely.

Experience has repeatedly confounded this expectation. Within a few years of a major road expansion, traffic frequently returns to its former level of congestion. Economists attribute this pattern to "induced demand." When a road becomes faster, the cost of using it, measured largely in time, declines, and people respond as they do to any reduction in price: they consume more. Drivers who previously traveled at other hours shift to peak times, others abandon public transportation, and some make trips they would formerly have forgone altogether.

A widely cited analysis of American cities found that the number of miles driven rose almost in exact proportion to the growth in road capacity, a relationship its authors dubbed "the fundamental law of road congestion." Over longer periods, the effect is compounded by changes in land use, as new highways encourage the construction of housing and businesses in outlying areas, generating yet more traffic.

The logic also operates in reverse. When roads have been closed or narrowed, whether by design or by disaster, the anticipated gridlock has often failed to materialize; some of the traffic simply evaporates as people alter their routines. Such findings have led many planners to conclude that congestion cannot be built away, and that pricing roads, improving public transit or managing demand in other ways offers more durable relief.

rc.title: Do Two Languages Make a Sharper Mind?
paras: A bilingual speaker never entirely switches off either language. Experiments tracking eye movements have shown that when bilinguals hear a word in one language, words that sound similar in their other language are briefly activated as well. Managing this constant competition, some researchers proposed, might function as a form of mental exercise, strengthening the so-called executive functions that allow us to focus attention, ignore distractions and shift between tasks.

Early studies appeared to confirm the idea. Bilingual children and adults were reported to outperform monolinguals on tasks that required them to suppress an automatic response, such as naming the color of the ink in which a conflicting word was printed. Some studies even suggested that lifelong bilingualism might delay the onset of dementia by several years. Such findings attracted wide publicity and were often presented as a compelling reason for parents to raise their children with two languages.

In the past decade, however, the bilingual advantage has become the subject of intense controversy. Several large-scale studies, involving thousands of participants, have found no reliable differences between bilinguals and monolinguals on measures of executive function. Critics have also pointed out that the earlier positive results may have been inflated by small samples and by the tendency of journals to publish studies that find effects while overlooking those that do not. Moreover, bilinguals and monolinguals often differ in immigration history, income and education, factors that are difficult to disentangle from language itself.

None of this diminishes the value of speaking two languages, which opens access to other cultures, communities and opportunities. What remains doubtful is the narrower claim that bilingualism confers a general cognitive boost. The episode has become something of a cautionary tale about how attractive hypotheses can outrun the evidence that supports them.

rc.title: The Language of Bees
paras: A honeybee that has found a rich source of food faces a problem: how can it tell the other bees in its hive where to go? In the 1940s, the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch discovered the answer. After years of patient observation, he showed that returning bees perform a special dance on the surface of the honeycomb, and that this dance contains precise information about the location of the food. For this work he shared the Nobel Prize in 1973.

The most informative form is the so-called waggle dance. The bee runs in a straight line while shaking its body from side to side, then circles back to its starting point and repeats the movement many times. The direction of the straight run tells the other bees which way to fly. Because the hive is dark, the dancer uses gravity as a reference: a run straight up the comb means "fly toward the sun," while a run at an angle to the right of vertical means "fly at that same angle to the right of the sun."

Distance is communicated as well. The longer the bee waggles during each run, the farther away the food lies. Other bees follow the dancer closely, sensing its movements in the dark, and then set out on their own. Remarkably, they are able to find the source even when it is more than a kilometer away.

Von Frisch's findings were met with skepticism at first, since many scientists doubted that an insect could use such an abstract code. Later experiments, including some using robotic bees that performed artificial dances, confirmed that the dance alone can direct bees to a particular spot. Today the waggle dance is regarded as one of the most sophisticated systems of communication known in the animal world.

rc.title: Movable Type Before Gutenberg
paras: Johannes Gutenberg's printing press, developed in Mainz around 1450, is commonly credited with launching a revolution in the dissemination of knowledge. It is less widely appreciated that movable type had been invented in East Asia centuries earlier. Around 1040, according to a near-contemporary account, a Chinese artisan named Bi Sheng fashioned individual characters from baked clay, and by the thirteenth century Korean printers were casting type in metal. The oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type, a Korean Buddhist text known as the Jikji, dates from 1377, nearly eight decades before Gutenberg's Bible.

Why, then, did the technology not transform East Asian societies as dramatically as it did Europe? Part of the answer lies in the nature of the writing systems involved. Gutenberg could print any Latin text with a few dozen letters and symbols, whereas a printer of Chinese required many thousands of distinct characters, each of which had to be manufactured, stored and retrieved. For many purposes, carving an entire page onto a single wooden block remained more economical, and woodblock printing continued to dominate in China for centuries.

Social and economic conditions mattered as well. In Korea, metal-type printing was largely a state enterprise, producing limited editions of official and religious texts for a small educated elite. In Europe, by contrast, printing quickly became a commercial venture. Competing printers, eager to recover their investments, sought out profitable markets, producing pamphlets, grammars and devotional works in large quantities and increasingly in local languages rather than Latin.

The comparison suggests that the consequences of a technology are not determined by the technology alone. The same fundamental invention may remain marginal in one setting and become transformative in another, depending on the writing system it serves, the institutions that control it and the economic incentives surrounding it. Historians who attribute the European transformation to the press itself, without regard to these circumstances, risk mistaking a necessary condition for a sufficient one.

rc.title: Climate Records Frozen in Ice
paras: The great ice sheets of Antarctica and Greenland are much more than vast stretches of frozen water. They are also archives. Each year, snow falls on their surface and is gradually pressed into ice by the weight of the layers above it. Over hundreds of thousands of years, this process has built up sheets more than three kilometers thick, in which the deepest layers are also the oldest.

To read this archive, scientists drill down into the ice and extract long cylinders called cores. As the snow turned into ice, it trapped tiny bubbles of air, and these bubbles are, in effect, samples of the atmosphere as it was when the ice formed. By analyzing them, researchers can measure the levels of gases such as carbon dioxide and methane in the distant past. One Antarctic core has provided a continuous record stretching back about 800,000 years.

The ice itself holds information too. The chemical makeup of the water molecules varies slightly with the temperature at the time the snow fell, allowing scientists to estimate past temperatures. Layers of volcanic ash can be matched with eruptions whose dates are already known, helping to date the ice around them, and the amount of dust trapped in each layer reveals how windy and dry the climate was.

Taken together, these records have revealed a striking pattern: over the past 800,000 years, carbon dioxide levels and temperatures have risen and fallen together through a series of ice ages and warmer periods. They also show that today's level of carbon dioxide is far higher than at any point in the entire record. For this reason, ice cores have become one of the most important sources of evidence in the study of climate change.
